videos.title: The Battery Boom Moving From Electric Cars to the Power Grid
videos.description:
Factories built to supply America’s electric-vehicle boom are getting a second life making batteries for the power grid.  As EV demand weakens and electricity demand from data centers and new factories strengthens, battery makers are shifting toward stationary storage, but the new market still relies on federal incentives and a supply chain that remains partly dependent on China. The shift is visible at TransGrid’s Atlas projects in Arizona, where the contractor Qcells is using LG Energy Solution’s US-made battery cells.

videos.title: Is American democracy safe? | Martin Wolf on the US midterms
videos.description:
As Americans prepare to vote in the November 3 midterm elections, FT chief economics commentator Martin Wolf asks what the result will mean for Donald Trump, the future of US democracy and America's place in the world. 

In the first of a six-part series of interviews with leading historians and political analysts, Martin speaks to the scholar and former Republican adviser Robert Kagan, who has spent a decade warning about Trump's authoritarian ambitions. 

They discuss how Trump has accumulated so much power, whether America's democratic institutions can still constrain him, and what might happen if Republicans lose control of Congress. Could these elections mark a turning point for American democracy or has the country already gone too far down the road towards authoritarianism?

videos.title: Trump Says There's Zero Chance of Replacing Susie Wiles
videos.description:
"Balance of Power" focuses on the intersection of politics and global business. On today's show, Mick Mulvaney, former acting White House Chief of Staff and Co-Founder of the Freedom Caucus, says the Trump administration “set” Katie Zacharia “up to fail” by not giving her enough preparation before she began her five-day tenure as White House press secretary. Suzanne Clark, President and CEO of the US Chamber of Commerce, says businesses want greater certainty, including faster permitting, more legal immigration, lower tariffs and additional trade agreements to open markets and make supply chains more consistent. Kendall Scudder, Texas Democratic party chair, says the party has built infrastructure it did not have in 2018, including recruiting more than 1,000 precinct chairs and coordinating candidates across the statewide ticket.

videos.title: Why More Americans Regret College And Homeownership
videos.description:
For generations, mortgages and student loans have been held up as textbook examples of “good debt,".This borrowing promises to  build wealth or increase your earning power over time. On the other side of the coin is so-called “bad debt”, things like auto loans or credit card debt that don’t provide a financial return over time. As the costs of buying a home and getting a degree have continued to climb, more Americans are questioning whether those “good debt” investments are actually paying off.

videos.title: The Tiny Robot Solving a Massive Underground Crisis | WSJ
videos.description:
In January, a collapsed sewer pipe outside Washington, D.C., spilled more than 240 million gallons of raw sewage into the Potomac River. It is likely the largest sewage spill in U.S. history, but just one of an estimated 75,000 across the country each year, according to the EPA.

As aging sewer networks struggle with growing populations and changing weather patterns, a team of engineers and professors in Europe is developing a robot designed to detect and potentially address problems before disaster strikes.

WSJ explains how the $9 million EU-funded PIPEON project is tackling the dark and perilous world beneath our streets.

6:16 What's next?

videos.title: Why There’s An ‘Extremely Fierce’ Battle For TSMC's Limited Chip Manufacturing Capacity
videos.description:
Unstoppable demand for AI is leading to a capacity crunch on factory lines at the world's leading chip manufacturer, Taiwan Semiconductor. And it could put a chokehold on AI's ability to scale. Analysts tell CNBC that Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom, AMD and others are locked in an “extremely fierce” competition to get their GPUs, CPUs and custom AI chips made at TSMC. Capacity can’t come online fast enough, despite TSMC’s rush to build new fabs in Taiwan, Japan and Arizona, where has expanded investment to $265 billion. The strain has made one man at TSMC “the most popular person on the planet,” as chip start-ups and big name CEOs visit Taiwan to ask him for wafer allocation. It’s also created a rich opportunity for Intel, as customers look to the long-struggling foundry arm of the U.S. chip manufacturer for a second source.

2:06 ‘Most popular person on the planet’
6:54 Making room for smaller players

TBWalmart, the world’s largest retailer, has been rolling out digital shelf labels in thousands of U.S. stores since 2024. The company says the technology streamlines price changes, frees up employees’ time and helps shoppers find what they need. But as the labels expand, so do concerns about dynamic pricing. CNBC’s Laya Neelakandan visits a Walmart store in New Jersey.
